section_summary: This section traces debates over Japanese Army reorganization, mechanization, manpower, expenditure, and disarmament from 1930 through mid-1932, including strong public and press opposition to military budgets during the Depression. It then documents the military’s growing independence from civilian authority during the Manchurian and Shanghai crises, threats against critics, fears of a coup or military-dominated government, and diplomatic efforts to restore civilian control. Later documents report Japanese commanders, deployments, combat performance, air-raid preparations, and operations in Shanghai, Tianjin, Harbin, and Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Binding slip for file 894.20/-11
subfiles.about: Identifies the bound archival unit as file 894.20/-11.
subfiles.summary: The slip bears the file number 894.20/-11 and the word “Bound.” It also carries the number 6273.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 103: Obstacles to reorganization and modernization of the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: Explains institutional resistance to General Ugaki's plan to modernize and reduce the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Castle describes the division of authority among the General Staff, Inspectorate of Military Education, and War Office, arguing that Ugaki could not reform the Army without the other chiefs' concurrence. The retirement of Soroku Suzuki and appointment of Kanaya improved the plan's prospects, but conservative resistance remained strong. The despatch connects Army policy to fears of Russia and China, domestic political economy, and the Army's role in inculcating loyalty to the Emperor.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Civilian and military authority over Army reorganization
subfiles.about: Points to Despatch No. 118 concerning the struggle between civilian and military elements over Army reorganization.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to another file for Castle's May 5 despatch. It notes that the civilian government had gradually acquired greater control over the Army's peacetime establishment since 1912.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Formation of the National Disarmament League
subfiles.about: References a report on a liberal political and business organization promoting further disarmament.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 131 and related political-report files. It identifies the subject as the organization of political liberals in support of further disarmament.

subfiles.title: Extract: Organization and program of the National Disarmament League
subfiles.about: Reports the creation of the Kokumin Genshuku Domei and its argument that military costs consumed an excessive share of Japan's budget.
subfiles.summary: The extract identifies Yukio Ozaki, Inazo Nitobe, and Daikichiro Tagawa as leaders of a new disarmament organization inaugurated on January 19. Its resolution calculates that military and naval budgets, pensions, and military-debt interest consumed roughly half of state expenditure. The league invited the public to support arms reductions and financial relief.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 225: Military Investigation Commission report and reaction to Army reform
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Army commission's reorganization proposals and the hostile public reaction to its failure to reduce military expenditure.
subfiles.summary: The commission proposed cutting about 25,000 enlisted men while retaining seventeen divisions and using approximately ¥8 million in savings for mechanization. Japanese newspapers protested that taxpayers would receive no relief and attacked the Army's institutional independence and economic priorities. The despatch also explains military arguments based on national prestige, threats from Russia and China, bargaining at the coming Geneva conference, and the Army's conservative social function.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Army Reform and the Military Investigation Committee
subfiles.about: References Despatch No. 240 on the proposed manpower reduction and reinvestment of savings in equipment.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes the committee's plan to reduce a force of about 200,000 by approximately 25,000 men. It notes that the resulting ¥8 million saving would be spent on mechanical equipment rather than returned to taxpayers.

subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 240: Public opposition to the Army reform report
subfiles.about: Summarizes press and public opposition to the Army's decision to reinvest personnel savings in military equipment.
subfiles.summary: The extract recounts expectations that the Military Investigation Committee would reduce the burden of armaments during the Depression. Instead, the decision to spend all personnel savings on mechanization produced a chorus of press criticism. The author concludes that the public was more concerned with taxation, economic distress, and peace than with military modernization or imperial expansion.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese Armaments Report
subfiles.about: References Despatch No. 351 concerning Japan's armaments report to the League of Nations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records that Japan filed the report on September 10 for use at the forthcoming arms conference. It indicates that the report supplied statistical information on Japanese forces.

subfiles.title: Extract: Statistics from Japan's League of Nations armaments report
subfiles.about: Lists personnel, naval tonnage, and aircraft figures submitted by Japan to the League of Nations.
subfiles.summary: The extract says Japan reported land, air, and naval personnel figures pursuant to a League Council resolution. It also gives totals for capital and auxiliary naval tonnage and for military and naval aircraft, although several numerals are degraded by OCR.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Failure of civilian government to restrain the military
subfiles.about: References a despatch on the civilian branches' failure to check Japanese military activity after September 18.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 383 in another file. Its subject is the inability of civilian authorities to restrain military operations following the Manchurian Incident.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Memorandum on Japanese military policy
subfiles.about: References a memorandum on factors obstructing demands for reduced Japanese armaments.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a State Department memorandum on Japanese military policy. It characterizes the factors discussed as a serious problem for Japanese advocates of arms reduction.

subfiles.title: Report on the Conscripts' Employment Guarantee Law
subfiles.from: Thomas C. Cramor, Assistant Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese legal protections for employees called to compulsory military service.
subfiles.summary: The report outlines requirements that private and government employers restore conscripts to their former positions after service and refrain from dismissing them solely because of military obligations. It lists exceptions involving failure to notify an employer, illness or wounds, criminal or disciplinary punishment, and the disappearance of the original work. It also describes penalties, mediation arrangements, and parallel protections for public employees.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Prince Kanin appointed Chief of the General Staff
subfiles.about: References a report on the appointment of Prince Kanin as Chief of the Japanese General Staff.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the appointment of an imperial prince to the Army's senior staff position. It emphasizes that Prince Kanin was a prince of the blood.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Tokyo editorial reaction to the Shanghai danger
subfiles.about: References a telegram on a Tokyo editorial urging calm amid the risk of clashes with foreign marines at Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Telegram No. 45. It describes the referenced editorial as advocating calm during a period of possible Japanese clashes with foreign marines.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 45: Tokyo press comment on Shanghai and military expenditure
subfiles.about: Reports Tokyo newspaper editorials on Shanghai, mediation proposals, and Japanese military expenditure.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo Asahi urged calm to prevent clashes involving Japanese and foreign marines, while the Chugai offered a veiled criticism of military spending. The Hochi objected to portions of the three-power proposals as one-sided despite professing support for reasonable mediation. Forbes observed that other reputable newspapers offered no editorial comment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Military difficulties over the Manchurian situation
subfiles.about: References a confidential despatch on difficulties within Japanese military circles over Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 472. It identifies the subject as military difficulties arising from the Manchurian situation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Sato's alarm over loss of civilian control
subfiles.about: References a confidential Geneva telegram reporting Sato's fear that Japanese military authorities had escaped civilian control.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to confidential Telegram No. 35 in the Sino-Japanese series. It highlights Sato's grave concern about unchecked Japanese military authority.

subfiles.title: Confidential Telegram No. 35: Japanese diplomats seek an end to the Shanghai hostilities
subfiles.about: Reports Sato and Matsudaira's concern that the Shanghai conflict threatened Japan's position and should be ended through international cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Sato told Gibson and Davis that operations at Shanghai had endangered Japan's position in Manchuria and forced a choice between escalation and cessation. He and Matsudaira favored a Japanese initiative to end hostilities with assistance from the United States and England, possibly under the Nine-Power Treaty. They feared that military authorities were out of control and wanted foreign policy restored to civilian hands.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Condition of Japanese armaments
subfiles.about: References Dawson's strictly confidential report on the state of Japanese armaments.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to Report W.D. 1007 in the Sino-Japanese file. Its stated subject is the condition of Japanese armaments.

subfiles.title: Forwarding letter for Dawson's confidential armaments report
subfiles.from: American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Paris
subfiles.about: Forwards a strictly confidential report by Warrington Dawson.
subfiles.summary: The brief letter transmits Dawson's report to the Secretary of State. Dates and report numbers in the OCR are inconsistent, but the surrounding file identifies the material with February 1932.

subfiles.title: Strictly Confidential Report W.D. 1007: Condition of Japanese armaments
subfiles.about: Relays British intelligence suggesting that Japan lacked sufficient modern equipment for an imminent general war.
subfiles.summary: Dawson reports secondhand information that Japan had fallen behind its normal postwar equipment-replacement program and had not brought the Army to full efficiency. His source believed Japan could not complete the required purchases within six months, leading the British government to discount the likelihood of a general Far Eastern war. Dawson also asked whether orders placed at Le Creusot might have been concealed under other national names.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Declining danger of a young-officer coup
subfiles.about: References a confidential report that the danger of a coup by younger Japanese Army officers was diminishing.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a confidential item in the Sino-Japanese file. It records Forbes's assessment that the immediate threat of a young-officer coup was lessening.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Possible Army intervention in Japan's domestic crisis
subfiles.about: References a telegram on the possible use of the Army to prevent political and social chaos in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Telegram No. 359 and mentions General Shirakawa's farewell message to troops returning from China. It frames the report around the possibility of military intervention in a worsening domestic crisis.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 359: Reports of domestic crisis and Shirakawa's message to returning troops
subfiles.about: Transmits a Reuters report that political paralysis and reactionary unrest might force the Japanese Army to assume temporary control.
subfiles.summary: The report says the Seiyukai government was failing to address Japan's economic, political, and social crisis while a faction maneuvered for a national government. It warns that the Army might intervene to forestall chaos or a fascist uprising. Shirakawa told returning soldiers to remain trained and ready to answer an immediate imperial call.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Menace of military domination
subfiles.about: References a confidential despatch on the danger of military domination of the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a confidential report in another decimal-file series. Its sole stated subject is the menace of military domination in Japan.

subfiles.title: Fragment of a Forbes despatch on military intimidation and the political crisis
subfiles.about: Describes threats against critics of the military, political murders, press intimidation, and efforts to form a government capable of restraining the Army.
subfiles.summary: Nitobe had received death threats after warning against military domination and was forced by officers to explain himself, while police investigated political murders involving revolvers purchased by Lieutenant Fujii. Forbes reports that Saionji was consulting Inukai, Araki, and Yoshizawa about a national government, although conservative figures believed foreign protests strengthened extremists. The despatch also discusses Dan's final views, anti-American propaganda, censorship and intimidation of Fleisher, alleged attempts against Shidehara, Inukai, and Wakatsuki, and diplomatic agreement that further forceful protests might lead toward war.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: McCoy's view of military planning in Manchuria
subfiles.about: References McCoy's belief that the Japanese military planned the Manchurian movement without informing Shidehara or the prime minister.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded sheet points to the associated Shanghai telegram. Its subject is McCoy's conclusion that civilian leaders were excluded from the planning of Japanese operations in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Confidential Shanghai telegram: League Commission itinerary and Japanese military control
subfiles.about: Reports the League Commission's planned tour and McCoy's conclusion that Japan's military independently planned the Manchurian operation.
subfiles.summary: McCoy outlined the commission's intended travel through Nanjing, Beijing, Manchuria, Japan, Korea, and China before drafting its report. He believed the Manchurian movement had been planned by the Japanese military without Shidehara or the prime minister being informed. Johnson added that military officers controlled the Shanghai negotiations and that Shigemitsu deferred to them.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Rumored Japanese troop concentration in Formosa
subfiles.about: References a report that Japan was concentrating 100,000 troops in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a State Department memorandum concerning Japanese troops in Formosa. The recorded rumor alleged a concentration of approximately 100,000 men.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Stimson's conversation with the Italian ambassador about Formosa
subfiles.about: References a conversation about the rumor that Japan had concentrated 100,000 men in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a memorandum of the Secretary's conversation with the Italian ambassador. Their subject was the reported Japanese troop concentration on Formosa.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Recall of Lieutenant General Kashii from Tianjin
subfiles.about: References a despatch reporting Kashii's impending relief as commander of Japanese troops at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that Kashii would be relieved on March 20 before completing his normal tour. It says he would return to Tokyo for duty at the War College.

subfiles.title: Extract from Tianjin Despatch No. 91: Kashii's transfer and cordial Sino-Japanese contacts
subfiles.about: Reports Kashii's early transfer and an unusually cordial encounter between Chinese and Japanese officials at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The extract confirms that Kashii would return to Tokyo before completing his tour, while stating that the significance of the transfer was unknown. It describes Wang Shu-chang and his adviser Hwang Tzen-fah speaking cordially with Kashii and the Japanese consul general at a Washington Birthday ball. Their behavior contrasted with the colder relations seen at previous public occasions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Doihara's promotion and prediction of victory over Russia
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting Doihara's promotion and his claim that Japan would defeat Russia in a war.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Doihara as newly appointed brigadier general and says he was going to Japan to command a brigade. It also records his prediction of a Japanese victory in any Russo-Japanese war.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 430: Conditions along the Chinese Eastern Railway and Doihara's promotion
subfiles.about: Transmits a Harbin report on disorder, Japanese troop movements, Soviet railway property, and Doihara's promotion.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports an unsuccessful attempt to blow up a railway bridge, widespread plunder and mistreatment, and a Japanese withdrawal designed to demonstrate the inability of New Kirin troops to maintain order. It also describes a dispute over locomotives allegedly retained by Soviet railway officials. Doihara announced his promotion, departure for a brigade command in Japan, and confidence that Japan would defeat Russia.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Poor Japanese combat performance at Shanghai
subfiles.about: References Despatch No. 1458 concerning the poor showing of Japanese land and naval forces during the Shanghai fighting.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a report on Japanese combat performance at Shanghai. It records foreign observers' unfavorable assessment of both the Army and Navy.

subfiles.title: Extract: Foreign observers' assessment of Japanese forces at Shanghai
subfiles.about: States that foreign military observers believed Japanese forces had performed poorly and had been overrated.
subfiles.summary: The brief extract says observers were amazed by Japan's poor showing during the Shanghai hostilities. It concludes that both the Japanese Army and Navy had been considerably overrated.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Editorial on Japan's future diplomacy
subfiles.about: References a Nagasaki report on an editorial published after the triumphal return of military and naval units from Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the editorial as “Japan's Future Diplomacy and Its Slogan.” It links its publication to successive triumphal receptions for forces returning from Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Kashii succeeded by Nakamura at Tianjin
subfiles.about: References a despatch on the Tianjin command change and growing opposition in Japan to the Shanghai operation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records Kashii's March 19 departure for Japan and succession by Major General K. Nakamura. It also notes reports of considerable opposition within Japan to military operations at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Extract from Tianjin Despatch No. 103: More conciliatory Japanese conduct
subfiles.about: Links Kashii's recall to a more conciliatory Japanese posture in Tianjin and domestic opposition to the Shanghai campaign.
subfiles.summary: The extract suggests that Kashii's premature transfer coincided with the League Commission's arrival and growing Japanese opposition to operations at Shanghai. Japanese officials at Tianjin had become markedly less aggressive and more conciliatory. Armed escorts on passenger trains and troop incursions beyond the concession had been reduced or nearly abandoned.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Younger officers reject party government
subfiles.about: References a telegram on younger Army officers' refusal to accept a party government.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the military attitude toward a party cabinet as its subject. It says younger officers remained adamant in their opposition.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 553: Army opposition to a party cabinet
subfiles.about: Transmits a Nippon Dempo report that younger officers were obstructing formation of a Suzuki party government.
subfiles.summary: The younger officers forming the military clique's backbone were said to reject any government controlled by an existing political party. Araki and Vice Chief Mazaki were reportedly unable to persuade them, leaving senior military leaders in a dilemma. A group of officers submitted thirteen demands concerning the new cabinet.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Municipal air-raid defense planning
subfiles.about: References a despatch on air-defense planning by officials in Osaka, Nagoya, and Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 600. It describes meetings to implement elaborate plans for defending three major cities against air attack.

subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 600: Anti-air-raid defenses
subfiles.about: Reports new municipal plans for defending Osaka, Nagoya, and Tokyo against aerial attack.
subfiles.summary: City officials met to put elaborate air-defense schemes into effect. The plans formed part of a sudden enthusiasm for aerial defense that also encouraged public subscriptions to buy aircraft for the Army.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Reported death of General Shirakawa
subfiles.about: References a Shanghai telegram disputing an early report of General Shirakawa's death.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records information from the Japanese consul general. It says the report of Shirakawa's death was, at minimum, premature.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 262: Shirakawa death report called premature
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese consul general's statement that General Shirakawa had not yet died.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham relays the consul general's denial of the reported death. He states that the report was “to say the least, premature” and repeats the information to the Legation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Conflicts within Japan and the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: References Dr. Lo's account of conflict between military and civilians and between the home Army and the Army in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Lo distinguished a civil-military struggle within Japan from a conflict between Army leaders at home and commanders in Manchuria. He believed the home faction was ambitious but less expansive than General Honjo and his followers.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: McCoy's assessment of the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: References remarks by Major General Frank R. McCoy about the Japanese Army as a fighting machine.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Despatch No. 1581 concerning a June 10 conversation between McCoy and Minister Johnson. Its subject is McCoy's evaluation of the Japanese Army's combat effectiveness.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Reinforcement of Japanese forces in Manchuria
subfiles.about: References a Mukden report on the dispatch of Matsuki's division against Ma Zhanshan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet reports that a Japanese division under Lieutenant General Matsuki reinforced the forces in Manchuria. The division was sent north to participate in the drive against Ma Zhanshan.

subfiles.title: Extract: Japanese deployments against Ma Zhanshan and Yalu-area insurgents
subfiles.about: Describes the movement of Japanese divisions in Manchuria and deteriorating reliability among Manchukuo troops.
subfiles.summary: The 14th Utsunomiya Division under Matsuki moved from Shanghai to northern Manchuria for operations against Ma Zhanshan before the rainy season. The 39th Brigade of the Chosen Division returned to Korea for action against bandits and secret societies near the Yalu River. The extract notes frequent insurgent activity, defections among Manchukuo troops, and Doihara's prominence as a Japanese authority on Chinese affairs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese troop strength and expansion in Manchuria
subfiles.about: References a memorandum on Japanese troop numbers in Manchuria and Japan's stated reasons for extending operations.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a State Department memorandum filed in the Sino-Japanese series. It identifies the memorandum's subjects as troop strength and the justifications offered for wider operations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese aircraft and troop movements toward Harbin
subfiles.about: References a Harbin report on Japanese forces pressing Old Kirin troops northward.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies movements of Japanese airplanes and soldiers into the Harbin area. Their purpose was to support operations driving the Old Kirin forces farther north.

subfiles.title: Extract: Japanese operations against Old Kirin forces
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese intervention after New Kirin forces failed to drive their opponents north and northeast.
subfiles.summary: Press claims of New Kirin successes were reportedly unsupported, prompting the Japanese command to operate in greater force. Tamon's headquarters moved forward, additional aircraft reached Harbin, and troops were drawn from another garrison that Old Kirin forces promptly reoccupied. The extract also reports an attack on a derailed Japanese armored train and casualties among Chinese and Japanese personnel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Withdrawal from Kungdah Mill
subfiles.about: References a Shanghai telegram reporting the withdrawal of the Japanese garrison from Kungdah Mill.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that Japanese troops had left the mill. It notes that Japan reserved the right to return them if deemed necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 354: Japanese withdrawal from Kungdah Mill
subfiles.about: Confirms the Japanese garrison's withdrawal from Kungdah Mill while noting Japan's claimed right to reoccupy it.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham reports that the garrison left the Kungdah Mill on Pingliang Road and that Boone verified the withdrawal. Japanese authorities reserved the right to send the troops back if necessary. The Joint Commission was informed by telephone, although Japan gave China no direct notice.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese military conferences at Kovalsky's house
subfiles.about: References a Harbin despatch on military conferences attended by Generals Honjo and Mazaki.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a series of important conferences at Mr. Kovalsky's house beside the Japanese Military Mission. Both General Honjo and General Mazaki, Assistant Chief of the General Staff, reportedly participated.
